\begin{aligned}
P(W_i^\alpha>x)
&=
P(W_i>x^{1/\alpha})\\
&=
e^{-x}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
W_i^\alpha\overset{d}=E_i,
\qquad
E_i\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1),
$$

or equivalently,

$$
\boxed{
W_i\overset{d}=E_i^{1/\alpha}.
}
$$

Define

$$
M_{E,n}:=\bigvee_{i=1}^nE_i
$$

and

$$
M_{W,n}:=\bigvee_{i=1}^nW_i.
$$

Since the function

$$
g(x)=x^{1/\alpha}
$$

is increasing on $(0,\infty)$,

$$
\boxed{
M_{W,n}
\overset{d}=
g(M_{E,n})
=
M_{E,n}^{1/\alpha}.
}
$$

From Example 8.1.2,

$$
M_{E,n}-\log n\Rightarrow Y,
$$

where $Y$ has the Gumbel distribution.

We therefore want to study

$$
g(M_{E,n})-g(\log n).
$$

However, the ordinary delta method in Section 8.3.1 is stated around a fixed
point, while here the centering point

$$
\theta_n=\log n
$$

satisfies

$$
\theta_n\to\infty.
$$

Thus we first justify the moving-center version of the delta method needed in
this exercise.

#### A moving-center delta method

Suppose

$$
X_n-\theta_n\Rightarrow Y,
\qquad
\theta_n\to\infty.
$$

Then

$$
X_n-\theta_n=O_P(1).
$$

Since $\theta_n\to\infty$,

$$
\frac{X_n-\theta_n}{\theta_n}
\xrightarrow{P}0,
$$

and therefore

$$
\boxed{
\frac{X_n}{\theta_n}\xrightarrow{P}1.
}
$$

Let $g$ be differentiable, and suppose $g'$ is eventually positive and
regularly varying at infinity with index $\rho$, that is,

$$
\frac{g'(tx)}{g'(x)}
\longrightarrow
t^\rho
\qquad
(x\to\infty)
$$

for every $t>0$.

By the mean value theorem, there exists a random $\xi_n$ lying between $X_n$
and $\theta_n$ such that

$$
g(X_n)-g(\theta_n)
=
g'(\xi_n)(X_n-\theta_n).
$$

Since $\xi_n$ lies between $X_n$ and $\theta_n$,

$$
\left|
\frac{\xi_n}{\theta_n}-1
\right|
\leq
\left|
\frac{X_n}{\theta_n}-1
\right|.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{
\frac{\xi_n}{\theta_n}\xrightarrow{P}1.
}
$$

Now write

$$
T_n:=\frac{\xi_n}{\theta_n}.
$$

Then

$$
T_n\xrightarrow{P}1.
$$

Since $g'$ is regularly varying, the uniform convergence theorem for regularly
varying functions implies that, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of
$(0,\infty)$,

$$
\frac{g'(t\theta_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
-
t^\rho
\to0.
$$

Because $T_n\to_P1$, with probability tending to one $T_n$ lies in a compact
neighborhood of $1$. Therefore,

$$
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
=
\frac{g'(T_n\theta_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
\xrightarrow{P}
1^\rho
=
1.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{g(X_n)-g(\theta_n)}
{g'(\theta_n)}
&=
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}
{g'(\theta_n)}
(X_n-\theta_n).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
\xrightarrow{P}1
$$

and

$$
X_n-\theta_n\Rightarrow Y,
$$

Slutsky's theorem gives

$$
\boxed{
\frac{g(X_n)-g(\theta_n)}
{g'(\theta_n)}
\Rightarrow Y.
}
$$

Thus regular variation of $g'$ is a sufficient condition for this moving-center
delta method.

#### Apply it to the Weibull maximum

In the present exercise,

$$
X_n=M_{E,n},
\qquad
\theta_n=\log n,
$$

and

$$
M_{E,n}-\log n\Rightarrow Y.
$$

Take

$$
g(x)=x^{1/\alpha}.
$$

Then

$$
g'(x)
=
\frac1\alpha x^{1/\alpha-1}.
$$

Therefore $g'$ is regularly varying with index

$$
\rho=\frac1\alpha-1.
$$

Indeed, for every $t>0$,

$$
\frac{g'(tx)}{g'(x)}
=
\frac{
\frac1\alpha(tx)^{1/\alpha-1}
}{
\frac1\alpha x^{1/\alpha-1}
}
=
t^{1/\alpha-1}.
$$

Thus the moving-center delta method applies, and

$$
\frac{
g(M_{E,n})-g(\log n)
}{
g'(\log n)
}
\Rightarrow Y.
$$

Now

$$
g(M_{E,n})
=
M_{E,n}^{1/\alpha}
\overset{d}=M_{W,n},
$$

$$
g(\log n)
=
(\log n)^{1/\alpha},
$$

and

$$
g'(\log n)
=
\frac1\alpha
(\log n)^{1/\alpha-1}.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{
\frac{
M_{W,n}-(\log n)^{1/\alpha}
}{
\frac1\alpha(\log n)^{1/\alpha-1}
}
\Rightarrow Y.
}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\boxed{
\alpha(\log n)^{1-1/\alpha}
\left[
M_{W,n}-(\log n)^{1/\alpha}
\right]
\Rightarrow Y,
}
$$

where $Y$ has the Gumbel distribution.

$\textbf{Note:}$

Section 8.3.1 proves the delta method in a fixed-center setting. The proof there
uses local linearization around a fixed parameter.

In this exercise the center is instead

$$
\theta_n=\log n\to\infty.
$$

Therefore differentiability of $g$ alone is not enough to justify

$$
g(M_{E,n})-g(\log n)
\approx
g'(\log n)(M_{E,n}-\log n).
$$

The mean value theorem gives

$$
g(M_{E,n})-g(\log n)
=
g'(\xi_n)(M_{E,n}-\log n),
$$

so what is really required is

$$
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}{g'(\log n)}
\xrightarrow{P}1.
$$

Since

$$
\frac{\xi_n}{\log n}\xrightarrow{P}1,
$$

regular variation of $g'$ provides exactly this stability.

For this exercise,

$$
g'(x)
=
\frac1\alpha x^{1/\alpha-1}
$$

is regularly varying, and therefore the required derivative ratio converges to
$1$.

Thus the essential mechanism is

$$
M_{E,n}-\log n\Rightarrow Y
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\frac{M_{E,n}}{\log n}\to_P1
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\frac{\xi_n}{\log n}\to_P1
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}{g'(\log n)}\to_P1
\qquad
\text{(regular variation)}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\frac{
g(M_{E,n})-g(\log n)
}{
g'(\log n)
}
\Rightarrow Y.
$$

So the phrase ``use the delta method'' in this exercise hides an additional
moving-center argument that is not proved explicitly in Section 8.3.1.


$\textbf{Note 2:}$

In the step

$$
\frac{g(X_n)-g(\theta_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
=
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
(X_n-\theta_n),
$$

where $\xi_n$ lies between $X_n$ and $\theta_n$, suppose

$$
X_n-\theta_n\Rightarrow Y.
$$

Then

$$
X_n-\theta_n=O_P(1).
$$

Since $\xi_n$ lies between $X_n$ and $\theta_n$,

$$
\xi_n-\theta_n=O_P(1).
$$

Therefore, if we want

$$
\frac{g(X_n)-g(\theta_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
\Rightarrow Y,
$$

it is enough to have

$$
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
\xrightarrow{P}1.
$$

Thus we only need a local property of $g'$ in a bounded neighborhood of
$\theta_n$, rather than a global condition such as regular variation.

A convenient sufficient condition is that, for every $M<\infty$,

$$
\boxed{
\sup_{|h|\leq M}
\left|
\frac{g'(\theta_n+h)}{g'(\theta_n)}-1
\right|
\longrightarrow0.
}
$$

More generally, if $\theta_n\to\infty$, one may write the condition as

$$
\boxed{
\forall M<\infty,\qquad
\sup_{|h|\leq M}
\left|
\frac{g'(x+h)}{g'(x)}-1
\right|
\longrightarrow0,
\qquad x\to\infty.
}
$$

To see why this is sufficient, write

$$
\xi_n=\theta_n+H_n,
$$

where

$$
H_n=O_P(1).
$$

For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $M<\infty$ such that, for all sufficiently
large $n$,

$$
P(|H_n|>M)<\varepsilon.
$$

On the event $\{|H_n|\leq M\}$,

$$
\left|
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}-1
\right|
=
\left|
\frac{g'(\theta_n+H_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}-1
\right|
\leq
\sup_{|h|\leq M}
\left|
\frac{g'(\theta_n+h)}{g'(\theta_n)}-1
\right|.
$$

By the local stability assumption, the right-hand side converges to $0$.
Therefore,

$$
\frac{g'(\xi_n)}{g'(\theta_n)}
\xrightarrow{P}1.
$$

Since

$$
X_n-\theta_n\Rightarrow Y,
$$

Slutsky's theorem gives

$$
\boxed{
\frac{g(X_n)-g(\theta_n)}
{g'(\theta_n)}
\Rightarrow Y.
}
$$

So the moving-center delta method used in Exercise 34 does not require a global
condition on $g'$. What the proof actually needs is only that $g'$ be
asymptotically stable on bounded additive neighborhoods of $\theta_n$.

### Ex 16
::: problem

Suppose $\{X_n,n\geq1\}$ are iid non-negative random variables and set

$$
M_n=\bigvee_{i=1}^n X_i,\qquad n\geq1.
$$

Show that there exists a sequence $a_n>0$ such that, for $x>0$,

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
P\left[\frac{M_n}{a_n}\leq x\right]
=
\exp\{-x^{-\alpha}\},
\qquad
x>0,\ \alpha>0,
$$

iff the regular variation condition holds:

$$
\lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{P[X_1>tx]}{P[X_1>t]}
=
x^{-\alpha},
\qquad
x>0.
\tag{8.30}
$$

In this case, what limit distribution exists for $\log M_n$? For $M_n^2$?

Verify (8.30) for the Cauchy density and the Pareto distribution?

:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Let

$$
S(x):=P(X_1>x)=1-F(x)
$$

be the survival function.

We first prove the equivalence

$$
\boxed{
\frac{M_n}{a_n}\Rightarrow\Phi_\alpha
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S\in RV_{-\alpha},
}
$$

where

$$
\Phi_\alpha(x)=\exp\{-x^{-\alpha}\},
\qquad x>0.
$$

#### $(\Rightarrow)$

Suppose there exists $a_n>0$ such that

$$
\frac{M_n}{a_n}\Rightarrow\Phi_\alpha.
$$

Then, for fixed $x>0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(M_n\leq a_nx)
&=
F(a_nx)^n\\
&=
[1-S(a_nx)]^n\\
&\longrightarrow
\exp\{-x^{-\alpha}\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
nS(a_nx)\longrightarrow x^{-\alpha}.
}
\tag{1}
$$

In particular, taking $x=1$,

$$
\boxed{
nS(a_n)\longrightarrow1.
}
\tag{2}
$$

Hence

$$
S(a_n)\to0,
$$

and from (1) and (2),

$$
\boxed{
\frac{S(a_nx)}{S(a_n)}
\longrightarrow
x^{-\alpha}.
}
\tag{3}
$$

For now, however, (3) only tells us the behavior of $S$ along the sequence
$\{a_n\}$. Our real goal is

$$
\frac{S(tx)}{S(t)}
\longrightarrow
x^{-\alpha},
\qquad t\to\infty.
$$

So we need a bridge from $\{a_n\}$ to arbitrary large $t$.

##### Step 1: $a_n\to\infty$

Let

$$
x_F:=\sup\{x:S(x)>0\}
$$

be the right endpoint of the distribution.

Suppose $a_n\not\to\infty$. Since $a_n>0$, there exists a subsequence
$\{a_{n_k}\}$ such that

$$
a_{n_k}\to a<\infty.
$$

Since

$$
S(a_{n_k})\to0,
$$

we consider the position of $a$ relative to $x_F$.

If $a<x_F$, choose $y$ such that

$$
a<y<x_F.
$$

Then

$$
S(y)>0.
$$

For sufficiently large $k$,

$$
a_{n_k}<y,
$$

and since $S$ is non-increasing,

$$
S(a_{n_k})\geq S(y)>0,
$$

contradicting $S(a_{n_k})\to0$.

If $a>x_F$, then for sufficiently large $k$,

$$
a_{n_k}>x_F,
$$

and therefore

$$
S(a_{n_k})=0,
$$

contradicting

$$
n_kS(a_{n_k})\to1.
$$

The remaining possibility is

$$
a=x_F.
$$

Take any $x\in(0,1)$. Then

$$
a_{n_k}x\to ax<x_F.
$$

Choose $y$ such that

$$
ax<y<x_F.
$$

For sufficiently large $k$,

$$
a_{n_k}x<y,
$$

so

$$
S(a_{n_k}x)\geq S(y)>0.
$$

But from (1),

$$
n_kS(a_{n_k}x)\to x^{-\alpha},
$$

which implies

$$
S(a_{n_k}x)\to0.
$$

This is again a contradiction.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
a_n\to\infty.
}
\tag{4}
$$

##### Step 2: $a_{n+1}/a_n\to1$

By assumption,

$$
\frac{M_{n+1}}{a_{n+1}}
\Rightarrow
Z,
\qquad
Z\sim\Phi_\alpha.
$$

We also have

$$
\frac{M_{n+1}}{a_n}
\Rightarrow
Z.
$$

Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(M_{n+1}\leq a_nx)
&=
F(a_nx)^{n+1}\\
&=
F(a_nx)^nF(a_nx).
\end{aligned}
$$

We know

$$
F(a_nx)^n\to\Phi_\alpha(x),
$$

and by (1),

$$
S(a_nx)\to0,
$$

so

$$
F(a_nx)\to1.
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{M_{n+1}}{a_n}
\Rightarrow
Z.
$$

Thus

$$
\frac{M_{n+1}}{a_{n+1}}
\Rightarrow
Z
$$

and

$$
\frac{M_{n+1}}{a_n}
\Rightarrow
Z.
$$

By the convergence to types theorem, there exists $A>0$ such that

$$
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\to A.
$$

Then

$$
AZ\overset{d}=Z.
$$

Since

$$
P(Z\leq x)
=
\exp\{-x^{-\alpha}\},
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(AZ\leq x)
&=
P\left(Z\leq\frac{x}{A}\right)\\
&=
\exp\left\{
-\left(\frac{x}{A}\right)^{-\alpha}
\right\}\\
&=
\exp\{-A^\alpha x^{-\alpha}\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

But $AZ\overset d=Z$, so

$$
A^\alpha=1.
$$

Since $A>0$,

$$
A=1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\to1.
}
\tag{5}
$$

So far, $\{a_n\}$ has the two properties we want:

$$
a_n\to\infty
$$

and

$$
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\to1.
$$

However, $\{a_n\}$ need not be monotone. To squeeze an arbitrary $t$ between
neighboring normalization points, we now construct a monotone sequence which
behaves asymptotically like $\{a_n\}$.

##### Step 3: Monotonization of $\{a_n\}$

Define

$$
b_n
:=
F^{\leftarrow}\left(1-\frac1n\right)
=
\inf\left\{
x:S(x)\leq\frac1n
\right\}.
$$

Since $1/n$ decreases with $n$ and $S$ is non-increasing,

$$
\boxed{
\{b_n\}\text{ is non-decreasing}.
}
$$

We now show that

$$
\boxed{
\frac{b_n}{a_n}\to1.
}
$$

Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.

From (1),

$$
nS((1+\varepsilon)a_n)
\longrightarrow
(1+\varepsilon)^{-\alpha}<1.
$$

Hence, for sufficiently large $n$,

$$
S((1+\varepsilon)a_n)<\frac1n.
$$

Since $b_n$ is the first point where $S$ reaches or falls below $1/n$,

$$
b_n\leq(1+\varepsilon)a_n.
$$

Similarly,

$$
nS((1-\varepsilon)a_n)
\longrightarrow
(1-\varepsilon)^{-\alpha}>1.
$$

Hence eventually

$$
S((1-\varepsilon)a_n)>\frac1n.
$$

Therefore the $1/n$ level has not yet been crossed at $(1-\varepsilon)a_n$,
so

$$
(1-\varepsilon)a_n<b_n.
$$

Thus

$$
1-\varepsilon
<
\frac{b_n}{a_n}
\leq
1+\varepsilon.
$$

Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{b_n}{a_n}\to1.
}
\tag{6}
$$

So $\{b_n\}$ is a monotonization of $\{a_n\}$.

From (4) and (6),

$$
b_n\to\infty.
$$

Also,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}
&=
\frac{b_{n+1}}{a_{n+1}}
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}
\frac{a_n}{b_n}\\
&\longrightarrow1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}\to1.
}
\tag{7}
$$

##### Step 4: Transfer the tail behavior from $a_n$ to $b_n$

From

$$
(1-\varepsilon)a_n<b_n\leq(1+\varepsilon)a_n
$$

and the fact that $S$ is non-increasing,

$$
S((1+\varepsilon)a_n)
\leq
S(b_n)
\leq
S((1-\varepsilon)a_n).
$$

Divide by $S(a_n)$:

$$
\frac{S((1+\varepsilon)a_n)}{S(a_n)}
\leq
\frac{S(b_n)}{S(a_n)}
\leq
\frac{S((1-\varepsilon)a_n)}{S(a_n)}.
$$

Using (3),

$$
(1+\varepsilon)^{-\alpha}
\leq
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\frac{S(b_n)}{S(a_n)}
$$

and

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\frac{S(b_n)}{S(a_n)}
\leq
(1-\varepsilon)^{-\alpha}.
$$

Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives

$$
\boxed{
\frac{S(b_n)}{S(a_n)}\to1.
}
$$

Together with (2),

$$
\boxed{
nS(b_n)\to1.
}
\tag{8}
$$

Now take fixed $x>0$.

Again,

$$
(1-\varepsilon)a_n<b_n\leq(1+\varepsilon)a_n
$$

implies

$$
S((1+\varepsilon)a_nx)
\leq
S(b_nx)
\leq
S((1-\varepsilon)a_nx).
$$

Multiplying by $n$ and using (1),

$$
((1+\varepsilon)x)^{-\alpha}
\leq
\liminf_{n\to\infty}nS(b_nx)
$$

and

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}nS(b_nx)
\leq
((1-\varepsilon)x)^{-\alpha}.
$$

Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$,

$$
\boxed{
nS(b_nx)\to x^{-\alpha}.
}
\tag{9}
$$

Combining (8) and (9),

$$
\boxed{
\frac{S(b_nx)}{S(b_n)}
\to
x^{-\alpha}.
}
\tag{10}
$$

Thus $\{b_n\}$ carries the same asymptotic tail behavior as $\{a_n\}$, but it
also has the monotonicity that we need.

##### Step 5: Extend the result from $\{b_n\}$ to arbitrary $t\to\infty$

For sufficiently large $t$, define

$$
n(t)
:=
\max\{n:b_n\leq t\}.
$$

Since $b_n\to\infty$, this is well-defined for sufficiently large $t$, and

$$
b_{n(t)}
\leq
t
<
b_{n(t)+1}.
$$

For simplicity, write $n=n(t)$.

Since $S$ is non-increasing,

$$
S(b_{n+1}x)
\leq
S(tx)
\leq
S(b_nx),
$$

and

$$
S(b_{n+1})
\leq
S(t)
\leq
S(b_n).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{S(b_{n+1}x)}{S(b_n)}
\leq
\frac{S(tx)}{S(t)}
\leq
\frac{S(b_nx)}{S(b_{n+1})}.
$$

For the lower bound,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{S(b_{n+1}x)}{S(b_n)}
&=
\frac{S(b_{n+1}x)}{S(b_{n+1})}
\frac{S(b_{n+1})}{S(b_n)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

By (10),

$$
\frac{S(b_{n+1}x)}{S(b_{n+1})}
\to
x^{-\alpha}.
$$

Also, from (8),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{S(b_{n+1})}{S(b_n)}
&=
\frac{(n+1)S(b_{n+1})}{nS(b_n)}
\frac{n}{n+1}\\
&\to1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the lower bound tends to $x^{-\alpha}$.

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{S(b_nx)}{S(b_{n+1})}
&=
\frac{S(b_nx)}{S(b_n)}
\frac{S(b_n)}{S(b_{n+1})}\\
&\to
x^{-\alpha}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by squeezing,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{S(tx)}{S(t)}
\to
x^{-\alpha},
\qquad t\to\infty.
}
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{
S\in RV_{-\alpha}.
}
$$

#### $(\Leftarrow)$

Now suppose

$$
\boxed{
\frac{S(tx)}{S(t)}
\to
x^{-\alpha},
\qquad t\to\infty,
}
\tag{11}
$$

for every fixed $x>0$.

We want to construct $a_n>0$ such that

$$
\frac{M_n}{a_n}\Rightarrow\Phi_\alpha.
$$

Define

$$
a_n
:=
F^{\leftarrow}\left(1-\frac1n\right)
=
\inf\left\{
x:S(x)\leq\frac1n
\right\}.
$$

The regular variation condition implies that $S$ has no finite right endpoint.
Hence, for every finite $M$,

$$
S(M)>0.
$$

For sufficiently large $n$,

$$
\frac1n<S(M),
$$

so the $1/n$ crossing occurs to the right of $M$:

$$
a_n>M.
$$

Since $M$ is arbitrary,

$$
\boxed{
a_n\to\infty.
}
\tag{12}
$$

By the definition of $a_n$, for every $t<a_n$,

$$
S(t)>\frac1n.
$$

Also, since $S$ is right-continuous,

$$
\boxed{
S(a_n)\leq\frac1n.
}
$$

Indeed, by the definition of the infimum, there exists a sequence
$x_m\downarrow a_n$ such that

$$
S(x_m)\leq\frac1n.
$$

Right continuity of $S$ then gives

$$
S(a_n)
=
\lim_{m\to\infty}S(x_m)
\leq
\frac1n.
$$

Thus

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}nS(a_n)\leq1.
$$

To obtain the lower bound, fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.

Since

$$
(1-\varepsilon)a_n<a_n,
$$

the definition of $a_n$ gives

$$
S((1-\varepsilon)a_n)>\frac1n.
$$

Therefore,

$$
nS((1-\varepsilon)a_n)>1.
$$

Now, because $a_n\to\infty$, regular variation gives

$$
\frac{S((1-\varepsilon)a_n)}{S(a_n)}
\to
(1-\varepsilon)^{-\alpha}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
nS(a_n)
&=
nS((1-\varepsilon)a_n)
\frac{S(a_n)}{S((1-\varepsilon)a_n)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}nS(a_n)
\geq
(1-\varepsilon)^\alpha.
$$

Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$,

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}nS(a_n)\geq1.
$$

Together with the upper bound,

$$
\boxed{
nS(a_n)\to1.
}
\tag{13}
$$

Now, for fixed $x>0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
nS(a_nx)
&=
nS(a_n)
\frac{S(a_nx)}{S(a_n)}\\
&\longrightarrow
1\cdot x^{-\alpha},
\end{aligned}
$$

by (11) and (13).

Thus

$$
\boxed{
nS(a_nx)\to x^{-\alpha}.
}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\left(\frac{M_n}{a_n}\leq x\right)
&=
P(M_n\leq a_nx)\\
&=
F(a_nx)^n\\
&=
[1-S(a_nx)]^n\\
&\longrightarrow
\exp\{-x^{-\alpha}\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{M_n}{a_n}
\Rightarrow
\Phi_\alpha.
}
$$

Combining the two directions,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{M_n}{a_n}\Rightarrow\Phi_\alpha
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S\in RV_{-\alpha}.
}
$$

$\textbf{Note:}$

The difficult part of the $(\Rightarrow)$ direction is the difference between

$$
\frac{S(a_nx)}{S(a_n)}
\to x^{-\alpha}
$$

and the actual definition of regular variation,

$$
\frac{S(tx)}{S(t)}
\to x^{-\alpha}
\qquad(t\to\infty).
$$

The first statement only gives the asymptotic behavior along the normalization
sequence $\{a_n\}$.

The bridge is

$$
\frac{M_n}{a_n}\Rightarrow\Phi_\alpha
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
nS(a_nx)\to x^{-\alpha}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
a_n\to\infty,
\qquad
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\to1
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{construct the monotone sequence }
b_n=F^{\leftarrow}\left(1-\frac1n\right)
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\frac{b_n}{a_n}\to1
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\frac{S(b_nx)}{S(b_n)}
\to x^{-\alpha}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{squeeze arbitrary }t
\text{ between }b_n\text{ and }b_{n+1}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
S\in RV_{-\alpha}.
$$

Thus $\{b_n\}$ acts as a **monotonization** of the original normalization
sequence $\{a_n\}$.

In the $(\Leftarrow)$ direction, one should not simply assume

$$
S(a_n)=\frac1n,
$$

because the distribution may have jumps. The correct argument uses the first
crossing definition of $a_n$, right continuity of $S$, and an
$\varepsilon$-squeeze to prove

$$
nS(a_n)\to1.
$$


### Ex 28
::: problem

Let $x\in(0,1)$ have binary expansion

$$
x=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{d_n}{2^n}.
$$

Set

$$
f_n(x)=
\begin{cases}
2, & d_n=0,\\
1, & d_n=1.
\end{cases}
$$

Then show

$$
\int_0^1 f_n(x)\,dx=1
$$

so that $f_n$ is a density. The sequence $f_n$ only converges on a set of
Lebesgue measure $0$. If $X_n$ is a random variable with density $f_n$, then

$$
X_n\Rightarrow U,
$$

where $U$ is $U(0,1)$.

:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

$\textbf{Typo in the exercise:}$

The second branch of $f_n$ is printed as $1$, but this cannot be correct, since
then

$$
\int_0^1 f_n(x)\,dx
=
2\cdot\frac12+1\cdot\frac12
=
\frac32.
$$

The intended definition should be

$$
\boxed{
f_n(x)=
\begin{cases}
2, & d_n=0,\\
0, & d_n=1.
\end{cases}
}
$$

We use this corrected version below.

For every fixed $n$, the $n$-th binary digit is $0$ on half of $(0,1)$ and
$1$ on the other half. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx
&=
2\,\lambda\{x:d_n(x)=0\}
+
0\,\lambda\{x:d_n(x)=1\}\\
&=
2\cdot\frac12\\
&=
1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f_n$ is a density.

Now $f_n(x)\in\{0,2\}$. Therefore, for fixed $x$, the sequence
$\{f_n(x)\}$ converges only if it is eventually constant, which means that the
binary expansion of $x$ is eventually all $0$'s or eventually all $1$'s.

The collection of such $x$ is countable. Hence

$$
\boxed{
\lambda\{x:f_n(x)\text{ converges}\}=0.
}
$$

It remains to show that nevertheless

$$
X_n\Rightarrow U(0,1).
$$

Define

$$
f_n(x)=1+h_n(x),
$$

where

$$
h_n(x)=
\begin{cases}
1, & d_n(x)=0,\\
-1, & d_n(x)=1.
\end{cases}
$$

Let $g$ be any continuous function on $[0,1]$. Since $[0,1]$ is compact,
$g$ is uniformly continuous.

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1g(x)f_n(x)\,dx
&=
\int_0^1g(x)\,dx
+
\int_0^1g(x)h_n(x)\,dx.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1_{[0,1]}$ is the density of $U(0,1)$, it is enough to prove

$$
\boxed{
\int_0^1g(x)h_n(x)\,dx\to0.
}
$$

For each $n$, divide $[0,1)$ into $2^n$ subintervals

$$
I_{j,n}
=
\left[
\frac{j}{2^n},
\frac{j+1}{2^n}
\right),
\qquad
j=0,\ldots,2^n-1.
$$

Each interval has length $2^{-n}$.

For $n=1$, the binary digit $d_1$ is $0$ on the first interval and $1$ on
the second interval, so $h_1$ takes the values

$$
1,-1.
$$

For $n=2$, the four intervals correspond to the binary beginnings

$$
00,\ 01,\ 10,\ 11,
$$

so again the second digit alternates between $0$ and $1$, and $h_2$ takes the
values

$$
1,-1,1,-1.
$$

In general, $h_n$ alternates between $1$ and $-1$ on consecutive intervals:

$$
1,-1,1,-1,\ldots.
$$

Therefore we pair the intervals

$$
I_{2j,n},\qquad I_{2j+1,n},
\qquad
j=0,\ldots,2^{n-1}-1.
$$

On the first interval of each pair,

$$
h_n=1,
$$

while on the second,

$$
h_n=-1.
$$

Hence the contribution from one pair is

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{I_{2j,n}}g(x)h_n(x)\,dx
+
\int_{I_{2j+1,n}}g(x)h_n(x)\,dx\\
&=
\int_{I_{2j,n}}g(x)\,dx
-
\int_{I_{2j+1,n}}g(x)\,dx.
\end{aligned}
$$

By the integral mean-value theorem, there exist

$$
\xi_{j,0}\in I_{2j,n},
\qquad
\xi_{j,1}\in I_{2j+1,n},
$$

such that

$$
\int_{I_{2j,n}}g(x)\,dx
=
\frac1{2^n}g(\xi_{j,0}),
$$

and

$$
\int_{I_{2j+1,n}}g(x)\,dx
=
\frac1{2^n}g(\xi_{j,1}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_{I_{2j,n}}g(x)h_n(x)\,dx
+
\int_{I_{2j+1,n}}g(x)h_n(x)\,dx
=
\frac1{2^n}
\left[
g(\xi_{j,0})-g(\xi_{j,1})
\right].
$$

There are $2^{n-1}$ such pairs.

Also, since the two points lie in adjacent intervals,

$$
|\xi_{j,0}-\xi_{j,1}|
\leq
\frac{2}{2^n}
=
2^{1-n}.
$$

Since $g$ is uniformly continuous, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists
$\delta>0$ such that

$$
|x-y|<\delta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|g(x)-g(y)|<\varepsilon.
$$

For sufficiently large $n$,

$$
2^{1-n}<\delta.
$$

Thus, uniformly over all $j$,

$$
|g(\xi_{j,0})-g(\xi_{j,1})|
<
\varepsilon.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|
\int_0^1g(x)h_n(x)\,dx
\right|
&\leq
\sum_{j=0}^{2^{n-1}-1}
\frac1{2^n}
\left|
g(\xi_{j,0})-g(\xi_{j,1})
\right|\\
&\leq
2^{n-1}\frac1{2^n}\varepsilon\\
&=
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary,

$$
\boxed{
\int_0^1g(x)h_n(x)\,dx\to0.
}
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1g(x)f_n(x)\,dx
&=
\int_0^1g(x)\,dx
+
\int_0^1g(x)h_n(x)\,dx\\
&\longrightarrow
\int_0^1g(x)\,dx.
\end{aligned}
$$

That is,

$$
E[g(X_n)]
\longrightarrow
E[g(U)]
$$

for every continuous $g$ on $[0,1]$.

Therefore, by the Portmanteau theorem,

$$
\boxed{
X_n\Rightarrow U(0,1).
}
$$

$\textbf{Note:}$

This exercise gives an example where the densities themselves behave very
badly pointwise:

$$
f_n(x)\not\to1
$$

for Lebesgue-a.e. $x$.

In fact,

$$
|f_n(x)-1|=1
$$

for every $x$ outside the irrelevant binary-expansion ambiguity points, so

$$
\int_0^1|f_n(x)-1|\,dx=1
$$

for every $n$.

Thus there is neither almost-everywhere convergence of the densities nor
$L^1$ convergence to the uniform density.

Nevertheless,

$$
\int_0^1g(x)f_n(x)\,dx
\to
\int_0^1g(x)\,dx
$$

for every continuous test function $g$.

The reason is that the $+1$ and $-1$ oscillations of $h_n$ occur on smaller and
smaller dyadic intervals. Uniform continuity makes $g$ almost constant across
each neighboring pair, so the two contributions cancel asymptotically.

### Ex 11
::: problem

**Lévy metric.** For two probability distributions $F,G$, define

$$
d(F,G)
:=
\inf\left\{
\delta>0:
\forall x\in\mathbb R,\ 
F(x-\delta)-\delta
\leq G(x)
\leq F(x+\delta)+\delta
\right\}.
$$

Show this is a metric on the space of probability distribution functions
which metrizes weak convergence; that is,

$$
F_n\Rightarrow F_0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
d(F_n,F_0)\to0.
$$

:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

For convenience, define the set of admissible values

$$
D(F,G)
:=
\left\{
\delta>0:
\forall x\in\mathbb R,\ 
F(x-\delta)-\delta
\leq G(x)
\leq F(x+\delta)+\delta
\right\}.
$$

Then

$$
d(F,G)=\inf D(F,G).
$$

Notice first that $D(F,G)$ is non-empty. For example, every $\delta>1$ is
admissible, since all distribution functions take values in $[0,1]$.
Therefore $d(F,G)$ is well-defined and non-negative.

#### Part 1: $d$ is a metric

##### (i) Symmetry

Let

$$
\delta\in D(F,G).
$$

Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$
F(x-\delta)-\delta
\leq
G(x)
\leq
F(x+\delta)+\delta.
\tag{1}
$$

We want to show that the same $\delta$ is also admissible for $d(G,F)$.

From the upper inequality in (1), replace $x$ by $x-\delta$:

$$
G(x-\delta)
\leq
F(x)+\delta.
$$

Hence

$$
G(x-\delta)-\delta
\leq
F(x).
$$

From the lower inequality in (1), replace $x$ by $x+\delta$:

$$
F(x)-\delta
\leq
G(x+\delta).
$$

Therefore,

$$
F(x)
\leq
G(x+\delta)+\delta.
$$

Thus

$$
G(x-\delta)-\delta
\leq
F(x)
\leq
G(x+\delta)+\delta,
$$

so

$$
\delta\in D(G,F).
$$

Therefore,

$$
D(F,G)\subseteq D(G,F).
$$

By reversing the roles of $F$ and $G$,

$$
D(G,F)\subseteq D(F,G).
$$

Hence

$$
D(F,G)=D(G,F),
$$

and therefore

$$
\boxed{
d(F,G)=d(G,F).
}
$$

##### (ii) Identity of indiscernibles

First suppose

$$
F=G.
$$

For every $\delta>0$, since $F$ is non-decreasing,

$$
F(x-\delta)-\delta
\leq
F(x)
\leq
F(x+\delta)+\delta.
$$

Thus every $\delta>0$ is admissible, so

$$
\boxed{
d(F,F)=0.
}
$$

Conversely, suppose

$$
d(F,G)=0.
$$

Since the infimum of $D(F,G)$ is $0$, we can choose a sequence
$\delta_k\in D(F,G)$ such that

$$
\delta_k\downarrow0.
$$

For every $x$,

$$
G(x)
\leq
F(x+\delta_k)+\delta_k.
$$

Since $F$ is right-continuous,

$$
F(x+\delta_k)\to F(x),
$$

so

$$
G(x)\leq F(x).
$$

By symmetry,

$$
d(G,F)=0.
$$

Thus we may similarly choose admissible values tending to $0$ for $(G,F)$,
which gives

$$
F(x)\leq G(x).
$$

Therefore,

$$
F(x)=G(x)
\qquad
\forall x\in\mathbb R.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{
d(F,G)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F=G.
}
$$

##### (iii) Triangle inequality

Let $F,G,H$ be probability distribution functions.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose admissible $\delta_1,\delta_2$ such that

$$
\delta_1
<
d(F,G)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2},
$$

and

$$
\delta_2
<
d(G,H)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
$$

Since $\delta_1\in D(F,G)$,

$$
F(x-\delta_1)-\delta_1
\leq
G(x)
\leq
F(x+\delta_1)+\delta_1.
\tag{2}
$$

Since $\delta_2\in D(G,H)$,

$$
G(x-\delta_2)-\delta_2
\leq
H(x)
\leq
G(x+\delta_2)+\delta_2.
\tag{3}
$$

For the upper bound, substitute $x+\delta_2$ into the upper inequality of
(2):

$$
G(x+\delta_2)
\leq
F(x+\delta_2+\delta_1)+\delta_1.
$$

Using (3),

$$
\begin{aligned}
H(x)
&\leq
G(x+\delta_2)+\delta_2\\
&\leq
F(x+\delta_1+\delta_2)
+\delta_1+\delta_2.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the lower bound, substitute $x-\delta_2$ into the lower inequality of
(2):

$$
F(x-\delta_2-\delta_1)-\delta_1
\leq
G(x-\delta_2).
$$

Using (3),

$$
\begin{aligned}
H(x)
&\geq
G(x-\delta_2)-\delta_2\\
&\geq
F(x-\delta_1-\delta_2)
-(\delta_1+\delta_2).
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
F(x-(\delta_1+\delta_2))
-(\delta_1+\delta_2)
\leq
H(x)
\leq
F(x+(\delta_1+\delta_2))
+(\delta_1+\delta_2).
$$

Thus

$$
\delta_1+\delta_2\in D(F,H),
$$

and hence

$$
d(F,H)
\leq
\delta_1+\delta_2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
d(F,H)
<
d(F,G)+d(G,H)+\varepsilon.
$$

Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary,

$$
\boxed{
d(F,H)
\leq
d(F,G)+d(G,H).
}
$$

Thus $d$ is a metric.

---

#### Part 2: $d$ metrizes weak convergence

We prove

$$
F_n\Rightarrow F
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
d(F_n,F)\to0.
$$

##### $(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $F_n\Rightarrow F$

We want to prove

$$
d(F_n,F)\to0.
$$

Fix

$$
0<\varepsilon<1.
$$

We need to show that, for all sufficiently large $n$,

$$
F(x-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon
\leq
F_n(x)
\leq
F(x+\varepsilon)+\varepsilon
\tag{4}
$$

for **all** $x\in\mathbb R$ simultaneously.

The difficulty is that weak convergence only gives

$$
F_n(x)\to F(x)
$$

at individual continuity points of $F$. Therefore we need to turn the
pointwise information into a finite collection of conditions.

First choose continuity points

$$
A<B
$$

of $F$ such that

$$
F(A)<\frac{\varepsilon}{4},
\qquad
F(B)>1-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.
$$

This is possible because

$$
F(x)\to0
\qquad (x\to-\infty),
$$

and

$$
F(x)\to1
\qquad (x\to+\infty),
$$

while the set of discontinuities of a distribution function is at most
countable.

Inside the compact interval $[A,B]$, choose finitely many continuity points

$$
A=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_m=B
$$

such that

$$
x_{j+1}-x_j<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\qquad
(j=0,\ldots,m-1).
$$

Since

$$
F_n(x_j)\to F(x_j)
$$

for every $j$, and there are only finitely many $x_j$'s, there exists one
common $N$ such that, whenever $n\geq N$,

$$
|F_n(x_j)-F(x_j)|
<
\frac{\varepsilon}{4}
\qquad
(j=0,\ldots,m).
\tag{5}
$$

We now verify (4) in three regions.

##### Middle region: $A\leq x\leq B$

Choose $j$ such that

$$
x_j\leq x\leq x_{j+1}.
$$

Since $F_n$ is non-decreasing,

$$
F_n(x_j)
\leq
F_n(x)
\leq
F_n(x_{j+1}).
$$

For the lower bound, by (5),

$$
F_n(x)
\geq
F_n(x_j)
>
F(x_j)-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.
$$

Since

$$
x-x_j<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}<\varepsilon,
$$

we have

$$
x-\varepsilon<x_j.
$$

Hence, by monotonicity of $F$,

$$
F(x-\varepsilon)
\leq
F(x_j).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_n(x)
&>
F(x_j)-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\\
&\geq
F(x-\varepsilon)-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\\
&\geq
F(x-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the upper bound, again by (5),

$$
F_n(x)
\leq
F_n(x_{j+1})
<
F(x_{j+1})+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.
$$

Since

$$
x_{j+1}-x<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}<\varepsilon,
$$

we have

$$
x_{j+1}<x+\varepsilon.
$$

Thus

$$
F(x_{j+1})
\leq
F(x+\varepsilon).
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_n(x)
&<
F(x_{j+1})+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\\
&\leq
F(x+\varepsilon)+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\\
&\leq
F(x+\varepsilon)+\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore (4) holds for every $x\in[A,B]$.

##### Left tail: $x<A$

For the lower bound,

$$
F(x-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon
\leq
F(A)-\varepsilon
<
0
\leq
F_n(x).
$$

For the upper bound,

$$
F_n(x)
\leq
F_n(A).
$$

By (5),

$$
F_n(A)
<
F(A)+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}
<
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
$$

Since

$$
F(x+\varepsilon)\geq0,
$$

we get

$$
F_n(x)
<
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\leq
F(x+\varepsilon)+\varepsilon.
$$

Thus (4) also holds for $x<A$.

##### Right tail: $x>B$

For the upper bound,

$$
F_n(x)\leq1.
$$

Since

$$
F(x+\varepsilon)
\geq
F(B)
>
1-\frac{\varepsilon}{4},
$$

we certainly have

$$
F_n(x)
\leq
F(x+\varepsilon)+\varepsilon.
$$

For the lower bound,

$$
F_n(x)
\geq
F_n(B).
$$

By (5),

$$
F_n(B)
>
F(B)-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}
>
1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
$$

On the other hand,

$$
F(x-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon
\leq
1-\varepsilon
<
1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
F(x-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon
<
F_n(x).
$$

Thus (4) holds also for $x>B$.

We have therefore shown that, for all $n\geq N$,

$$
F(x-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon
\leq
F_n(x)
\leq
F(x+\varepsilon)+\varepsilon
\qquad
\forall x\in\mathbb R.
$$

Hence $\varepsilon$ is admissible for $d(F_n,F)$, so

$$
d(F_n,F)\leq\varepsilon.
$$

Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary,

$$
\boxed{
d(F_n,F)\to0.
}
$$

##### $(\Leftarrow)$ Suppose $d(F_n,F)\to0$

For each $n$, choose an admissible $\delta_n$ such that

$$
\delta_n
<
d(F_n,F)+\frac1n.
$$

Then

$$
\delta_n\to0.
$$

Since $\delta_n$ is admissible,

$$
F(x-\delta_n)-\delta_n
\leq
F_n(x)
\leq
F(x+\delta_n)+\delta_n
\qquad
\forall x\in\mathbb R.
\tag{6}
$$

Now fix

$$
x\in C(F),
$$

where $C(F)$ denotes the set of continuity points of $F$.

Since

$$
\delta_n\to0
$$

and $F$ is continuous at $x$,

$$
F(x-\delta_n)\to F(x)
$$

and

$$
F(x+\delta_n)\to F(x).
$$

Therefore the lower and upper bounds in (6) both converge to $F(x)$.

By squeezing,

$$
F_n(x)\to F(x).
$$

Thus

$$
F_n(x)\to F(x)
\qquad
\forall x\in C(F),
$$

which is exactly

$$
\boxed{
F_n\Rightarrow F.
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
F_n\Rightarrow F
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
d(F_n,F)\to0.
}
$$

Hence the Lévy metric metrizes weak convergence.

$\textbf{Note:}$

The main difficulty in the direction

$$
F_n\Rightarrow F
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
d(F_n,F)\to0
$$

is the difference between a pointwise statement and the requirement in the
definition of the Lévy metric.

Weak convergence gives

$$
F_n(x)\to F(x)
$$

only for each fixed $x\in C(F)$, whereas the Lévy metric requires one
$\varepsilon$-inequality that holds for

$$
\forall x\in\mathbb R
$$

simultaneously.

Choosing $x_L,x_R$ separately for each $x$ therefore gives an
$N=N(x,\varepsilon)$, which is not enough.

The repair is to choose finitely many continuity points on a compact middle
interval. Since there are only finitely many of them, one common $N$ works at
all grid points. Monotonicity then fills the gaps between grid points, while
the two tails are controlled by choosing $A$ and $B$ sufficiently far out.

Thus the key bridge is

$$
\text{pointwise convergence at continuity points}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{finite continuity grid}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{one common }N
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{uniform Lévy inequalities for all }x.
$$


### Ex 35
::: problem

Suppose $\{F_n,n\geq 0\}$ are probability distributions such that

$$
F_n\Rightarrow F_0.
$$

For $t>0$, let

$$
u_t(\cdot):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R
$$

be an equicontinuous family of functions that are uniformly bounded; that is,

$$
\sup_{t>0,\ x\in\mathbb R}|u_t(x)|\leq M
$$

for some constant $M$. Then show

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
=
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
$$

uniformly in $t$.

:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

What we want to show is

$$
\boxed{
\sup_{t>0}
\left|
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
\right|
\to0.
}
$$

The idea is to first control the tails by uniform boundedness, and then use
equicontinuity to reduce the compact middle part to finitely many interval
probabilities.

Fix $\eta>0$.

#### Step 1: Control the tails

Since

$$
F_n\Rightarrow F_0,
$$

choose $K>0$ sufficiently large such that

$$
-K,K\in C(F_0)
$$

and

$$
F_0([-K,K])>1-\eta.
$$

Since $[-K,K]$ is a continuity set of $F_0$,

$$
F_n([-K,K])
\to
F_0([-K,K]).
$$

Therefore, for all sufficiently large $n$,

$$
F_n([-K,K])>1-2\eta.
$$

Hence

$$
F_0(|x|>K)<\eta
$$

and eventually

$$
F_n(|x|>K)<2\eta.
$$

Since the family $\{u_t\}$ is uniformly bounded,

$$
|u_t(x)|\leq M
$$

for all $t>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$.

Thus, uniformly in $t$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&
\left|
\int_{|x|>K}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
\int_{|x|>K}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
\right|\\
&\qquad\leq
\left|
\int_{|x|>K}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
\right|
+
\left|
\int_{|x|>K}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
\right|\\
&\qquad\leq
M F_n(|x|>K)
+
M F_0(|x|>K)\\
&\qquad<
3M\eta.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

So the tail part has been controlled uniformly in $t$.

#### Step 2: Partition the compact middle part

Now consider the compact interval $[-K,K]$.

Since the family $\{u_t\}_{t>0}$ is equicontinuous, there exists
$\delta>0$, independent of $t$, such that

$$
|x-y|<\delta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|<\eta
$$

for every $t>0$.

The continuity set $C(F_0)$ is dense in $\mathbb R$, since the set of
discontinuities of a distribution function is at most countable.

Therefore, we can choose a finite partition

$$
-K=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_m=K
$$

such that

$$
x_j\in C(F_0),
\qquad j=0,\ldots,m,
$$

and

$$
x_j-x_{j-1}<\delta,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
$$

Define

$$
I_j=(x_{j-1},x_j],
\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
$$

Then

$$
[-K,K]
$$

is partitioned by the finitely many intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_m$, up to the
single endpoint $-K$, which causes no problem since $-K\in C(F_0)$.

For each $I_j$, choose some

$$
\xi_j\in I_j.
$$

Since the diameter of $I_j$ is less than $\delta$, for every $x\in I_j$,

$$
|u_t(x)-u_t(\xi_j)|<\eta
$$

uniformly in $t$.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&
\left|
\int_{I_j}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
u_t(\xi_j)F_n(I_j)
\right|\\
&=
\left|
\int_{I_j}
\left[u_t(x)-u_t(\xi_j)\right]F_n(dx)
\right|\\
&\leq
\eta F_n(I_j).
\end{aligned}
$$

Summing over $j$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&
\left|
\int_{[-K,K]}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
\sum_{j=1}^m u_t(\xi_j)F_n(I_j)
\right|\\
&\leq
\eta\sum_{j=1}^mF_n(I_j)\\
&\leq
\eta.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

The same argument gives

$$
\left|
\int_{[-K,K]}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
-
\sum_{j=1}^m u_t(\xi_j)F_0(I_j)
\right|
\leq
\eta.
\tag{3}
$$

Again, both bounds are independent of $t$.

#### Step 3: Compare the finite approximations

We now consider

$$
\begin{aligned}
&
\left|
\sum_{j=1}^m
u_t(\xi_j)F_n(I_j)
-
\sum_{j=1}^m
u_t(\xi_j)F_0(I_j)
\right|\\
&=
\left|
\sum_{j=1}^m
u_t(\xi_j)
\left[
F_n(I_j)-F_0(I_j)
\right]
\right|.
\end{aligned}
$$

By uniform boundedness,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&
\left|
\sum_{j=1}^m
u_t(\xi_j)
\left[
F_n(I_j)-F_0(I_j)
\right]
\right|\\
&\leq
M\sum_{j=1}^m
\left|
F_n(I_j)-F_0(I_j)
\right|.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$

The endpoints of each $I_j$ lie in $C(F_0)$, so every $I_j$ is a continuity
set of $F_0$. Hence, by weak convergence,

$$
F_n(I_j)\to F_0(I_j)
$$

for every $j=1,\ldots,m$.

There are only finitely many intervals. Therefore,

$$
\sum_{j=1}^m
\left|
F_n(I_j)-F_0(I_j)
\right|
\to0.
$$

Thus, for sufficiently large $n$,

$$
M\sum_{j=1}^m
\left|
F_n(I_j)-F_0(I_j)
\right|
<
\eta.
\tag{5}
$$

Importantly, the right-hand side of (4) does not depend on $t$.

#### Step 4: Combine the three parts

Using (1)--(5), for sufficiently large $n$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&
\left|
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
\right|\\
&\leq
\left|
\int_{|x|>K}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
\int_{|x|>K}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
\right|\\
&\quad+
\left|
\int_{[-K,K]}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
\sum_{j=1}^m u_t(\xi_j)F_n(I_j)
\right|\\
&\quad+
\left|
\sum_{j=1}^m
u_t(\xi_j)
\left[
F_n(I_j)-F_0(I_j)
\right]
\right|\\
&\quad+
\left|
\sum_{j=1}^m u_t(\xi_j)F_0(I_j)
-
\int_{[-K,K]}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
\right|\\
&<
3M\eta+\eta+\eta+\eta\\
&=
3M\eta+3\eta.
\end{aligned}
$$

Every bound above is independent of $t$. Therefore,

$$
\sup_{t>0}
\left|
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
\right|
<
3M\eta+3\eta
$$

for all sufficiently large $n$.

Since $\eta>0$ is arbitrary,

$$
\boxed{
\sup_{t>0}
\left|
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
-
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
\right|
\longrightarrow0.
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_n(dx)
\longrightarrow
\int_{\mathbb R}u_t(x)F_0(dx)
}
$$

uniformly in $t$.

$\textbf{Note:}$

Ordinary weak convergence tells us that for each fixed bounded continuous
function $u_t$,

$$
\int u_t\,dF_n
\to
\int u_t\,dF_0.
$$

The problem here is that $t$ ranges over an arbitrary, possibly uncountable,
family, so pointwise convergence in $t$ is not enough.

The two assumptions on $\{u_t\}$ play different roles.

Uniform boundedness,

$$
\sup_{t,x}|u_t(x)|\leq M,
$$

allows us to make the contribution outside a large compact interval uniformly
small.

Equicontinuity allows us, on that compact interval, to replace every $u_t$ by
its values at finitely many spatial points with an error that is uniform in
$t$.

Thus the proof reduces the whole uncountable family to finitely many
probability masses

$$
F_n(I_1),\ldots,F_n(I_m),
$$

and weak convergence handles these finitely many quantities simultaneously.

The structure is therefore

$$
\text{weak convergence}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{tightness / compact truncation}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{equicontinuity gives a finite spatial approximation}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{weak convergence on finitely many continuity intervals}
$$

$$
\Downarrow
$$

$$
\text{uniform convergence in }t.
$$

This is similar to the finite-grid argument in Ex 11: the main technical move
is to turn an infinite uniform requirement into finitely many conditions for
which one common $N$ can be chosen.

### Ex 15
::: problem
**(Weissman)** Suppose $Y_n$, $n\geq 1$ are random variables such that there
exist $a_n>0$, $b_n\in\mathbb R$ and
$$
P[Y_n\leq a_nx+b_n]\longrightarrow G(x),
$$
non-degenerate, and for each $t>0$
$$
P[Y_{[nt]}\leq a_nx+b_n]\longrightarrow G_t(x),
$$
non-degenerate. Then there exists $\alpha(t)>0$, $\beta(t)\in\mathbb R$ such
that
$$
G(x)=G_t(\alpha(t)x+\alpha(t))
$$
and $\alpha(t)=t^\theta$. If $\theta=0$, then
$$
\beta(t)=c\log t,
$$
and if $\theta\neq0$, then
$$
\beta(t)=c(1-t^\theta).
$$
:::
$\textbf{Answer:}$
$\textbf{Typo in the exercise statement:}$
The book introduces both $\alpha(t)$ and $\beta(t)$, but the displayed type
relation is printed as
$$
G(x)=G_t(\alpha(t)x+\alpha(t)).
$$
The second $\alpha(t)$ should be $\beta(t)$. We therefore prove
$$
\boxed{
G(x)=G_t(\alpha(t)x+\beta(t)).
}
$$

* Step 1: Put the normalizations into the affine group
Let $H$ be the group of positive affine transformations
$$
H
=
\left\{
h:x\mapsto ax+b:
a>0,\ b\in\mathbb R
\right\},
$$
with group operation given by composition.
Let $e$ denote the identity transformation,
$$
e(x)=x.
$$
For each $n$, define
$$
h_n(x)
=
\frac{x-b_n}{a_n}.
$$
Then the first assumption can be written as
$$
h_n(Y_n)\Rightarrow Z,
$$
where $Z$ has the non-degenerate distribution function $G$.
For fixed $t>0$, since $[nt]\to\infty$,
$$
h_{[nt]}(Y_{[nt]})
\Rightarrow Z,
$$
while the second assumption gives
$$
h_n(Y_{[nt]})
\Rightarrow Z_t,
$$
where $Z_t$ has the non-degenerate distribution function $G_t$.
Define
$$
\gamma_n(t)
:=
h_nh_{[nt]}^{-1}.
$$
Then
$$
h_n(Y_{[nt]})
=
\gamma_n(t)
\left(
h_{[nt]}(Y_{[nt]})
\right).
$$
Both limiting distributions are non-degenerate. Therefore, by the convergence
to types theorem, for every fixed $t>0$ there exists
$$
\gamma(t)\in H
$$
such that
$$
\boxed{
\gamma_n(t)\longrightarrow\gamma(t).
}
\tag{1}
$$
Write
$$
\gamma(t)(x)
=
\alpha(t)x+\beta(t),
\qquad
\alpha(t)>0.
$$
Since
$$
h_{[nt]}^{-1}(x)
=
a_{[nt]}x+b_{[nt]},
$$
we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_n(t)(x)
&=
h_nh_{[nt]}^{-1}(x)\\
&=
\frac{a_{[nt]}}{a_n}x
+
\frac{b_{[nt]}-b_n}{a_n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence
$$
\frac{a_{[nt]}}{a_n}
\longrightarrow
\alpha(t)
$$
and
$$
\frac{b_{[nt]}-b_n}{a_n}
\longrightarrow
\beta(t).
$$
Also,
$$
Z_t
\overset{d}{=}
\gamma(t)Z
=
\alpha(t)Z+\beta(t).
$$
Therefore,
$$
\begin{aligned}
G_t(\alpha(t)x+\beta(t))
&=
P\left(
\alpha(t)Z+\beta(t)
\leq
\alpha(t)x+\beta(t)
\right)\\
&=
P(Z\leq x)\\
&=
G(x).
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus
$$
\boxed{
G(x)
=
G_t(\alpha(t)x+\beta(t)).
}
\tag{2}
$$
As in the proof on p. 280, $\alpha(\cdot)$ and $\beta(\cdot)$ are Lebesgue
measurable, since they are pointwise limits of measurable step functions of
$t$.

* Step 2: In this exercise, $T=(0,\infty)$ immediately
Following Weissman, define
$$
T
:=
\left\{
t>0:
\gamma_n(t)
\text{ converges to an element of }H
\right\}.
$$
In the original argument, establishing the size of $T$ is one of the technical
parts of the proof.
However, in this exercise, $G_t$ is assumed to be non-degenerate for every
$t>0$.
Therefore the convergence to types argument in Step 1 applies to every
$t>0$, and hence
$$
\boxed{
T=(0,\infty).
}
\tag{3}
$$
In particular, for every $t>0$,
$$
t,\ t^{-1}\in T.
$$

* Step 3: Prove that neighboring normalizations are asymptotically equivalent
For fixed $t>0$, define
$$
\delta_n(t)
:=
h_n
h_{\left[
\frac{[nt]}{t}
\right]}^{-1}.
$$
We can factor this as
$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta_n(t)
&=
h_nh_{[nt]}^{-1}
\,
h_{[nt]}
h_{\left[
\frac{[nt]}t
\right]}^{-1}\\
&=
\gamma_n(t)
\gamma_{[nt]}(t^{-1}).
\end{aligned}
$$
By (3),
$$
\gamma_n(t)\to\gamma(t)
$$
and, since $[nt]\to\infty$,
$$
\gamma_{[nt]}(t^{-1})
\to
\gamma(t^{-1}).
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{
\delta_n(t)
\longrightarrow
\gamma(t)\gamma(t^{-1}).
}
\tag{4}
$$
Now take
$$
t=\frac12.
$$
Then
$$
\delta_n(1/2)
=
h_n
h_{\left[2[n/2]\right]}^{-1}.
$$
If $n=2m$ is even,
$$
2[n/2]=2m=n,
$$
so

$$
\delta_{2m}(1/2)
=
h_{2m}h_{2m}^{-1}
=
e.
$$
Thus $e$ is a limit point of the sequence $\{\delta_n(1/2)\}$.
But by (4), the whole sequence $\delta_n(1/2)$ already converges. Therefore
its limit must equal the limit of the even subsequence, namely $e$:
$$
\boxed{
\delta_n(1/2)\to e.
}
\tag{5}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\gamma(1/2)\gamma(2)=e.
$$
Now suppose $n=2m+1$ is odd. Then
$$
2[n/2]=2m=n-1,
$$
and therefore
$$
\delta_n(1/2)
=
h_nh_{n-1}^{-1}.
$$
Using (5),
$$
\boxed{
h_nh_{n-1}^{-1}\to e.
}
\tag{6}
$$
By taking finite products, for every fixed integer $g$,
$$
\boxed{
h_nh_{n+g}^{-1}\to e.
}
\tag{7}
$$
This is the key fact which allows us to ignore bounded errors created by the
integer-part operation.

* Step 4: Prove that $\gamma$ is a homomorphism
Fix $s,t>0$.
We have
$$
\gamma_n(ts)
=
h_nh_{[nts]}^{-1}.
$$
Insert the intermediate normalizations $h_{[nt]}$ and
$h_{[[nt]s]}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_n(ts)
&=
h_nh_{[nt]}^{-1}
\,
h_{[nt]}h_{[[nt]s]}^{-1}
\,
h_{[[nt]s]}h_{[nts]}^{-1}\\
&=
\gamma_n(t)
\gamma_{[nt]}(s)
R_n,
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
$$
where
$$
R_n
:=
h_{[[nt]s]}h_{[nts]}^{-1}.
$$
For the first two terms,
$$
\gamma_n(t)\to\gamma(t)
$$
and, since $[nt]\to\infty$,
$$
\gamma_{[nt]}(s)\to\gamma(s).
$$
It remains to show
$$
R_n\to e.
$$
Since
$$
[nt]\leq nt<[nt]+1,
$$
multiplying by $s>0$ gives
$$
[nt]s
\leq
nts
<
[nt]s+s.
$$
Therefore
$$
0
\leq
[nts]-[[nt]s]
\leq
\lceil s\rceil.
$$
Thus the difference between the two indices is bounded by a fixed integer
independent of $n$.
By (7),
$$
\boxed{
R_n
=
h_{[[nt]s]}h_{[nts]}^{-1}
\longrightarrow e.
}
$$
Taking limits in (8),
$$
\boxed{
\gamma(ts)
=
\gamma(t)\gamma(s).
}
\tag{9}
$$
Thus
$$
\gamma:(0,\infty)\to H
$$
is a group homomorphism.
Since
$$
ts=st,
$$
we also have
$$
\gamma(t)\gamma(s)
=
\gamma(s)\gamma(t).
$$
Thus the image of $\gamma$ is a commutative subgroup of $H$.

* Step 5: Obtain the functional equations for $\alpha$ and $\beta$
Recall
$$
\gamma(t)(x)
=
\alpha(t)x+\beta(t).
$$
By (9),
$$
\gamma(ts)
=
\gamma(t)\gamma(s).
$$
The right-hand side is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma(t)(\gamma(s)(x))
&=
\alpha(t)
\left[
\alpha(s)x+\beta(s)
\right]
+
\beta(t)\\
&=
\alpha(t)\alpha(s)x
+
\alpha(t)\beta(s)
+
\beta(t).
\end{aligned}
$$
Comparing this with

$$
\gamma(ts)(x)
=
\alpha(ts)x+\beta(ts),
$$
we obtain

$$
\boxed{
\alpha(ts)
=
\alpha(t)\alpha(s)
}
\tag{10}
$$
and

$$
\boxed{
\beta(ts)
=
\alpha(t)\beta(s)+\beta(t).
}
\tag{11}
$$
Since $ts=st$,
$$
\boxed{
\beta(ts)
=
\alpha(s)\beta(t)+\beta(s).
}
\tag{12}
$$
These are exactly the functional equations used on p. 281.

* Step 6: Solve the functional equations
Since $\alpha$ is positive, measurable, and satisfies
$$
\alpha(ts)
=
\alpha(t)\alpha(s),
$$
the measurable Hamel equation gives
$$
\boxed{
\alpha(t)=t^\theta
}
$$
for some $\theta\in\mathbb R$.
We now consider two cases.

##### Case 1: $\theta=0$
Then
$$
\alpha(t)\equiv1.
$$
Equation (11) becomes
$$
\beta(ts)
=
\beta(t)+\beta(s).
$$
Define
$$
q(x)
:=
\beta(e^x).
$$
Then
$$
q(x+y)
=
q(x)+q(y).
$$
Since $q$ is measurable, the measurable Cauchy equation gives
$$
q(x)=cx
$$
for some $c\in\mathbb R$.
Therefore
$$
\boxed{
\beta(t)=c\log t.
}
$$

##### Case 2: $\theta\neq0$
Since
$$
\alpha(t)=t^\theta,
$$
equations (11) and (12) give
$$
\alpha(t)\beta(s)+\beta(t)
=
\alpha(s)\beta(t)+\beta(s).
$$
Thus
$$
\beta(t)(1-\alpha(s))
=
\beta(s)(1-\alpha(t)).
$$
Choose some $s_0\neq1$. Since $\theta\neq0$,
$$
\alpha(s_0)=s_0^\theta\neq1.
$$
Therefore
$$
\beta(t)
=
\frac{\beta(s_0)}
{1-\alpha(s_0)}
\left(
1-\alpha(t)
\right).
$$
Writing
$$
c
:=
\frac{\beta(s_0)}
{1-\alpha(s_0)},
$$
we obtain
$$
\boxed{
\beta(t)
=
c(1-t^\theta).
}
$$
Therefore
$$
\boxed{
\alpha(t)=t^\theta,
}
$$
and
$$
\boxed{
\beta(t)
=
\begin{cases}
c\log t, & \theta=0,\\[1mm]
c(1-t^\theta), & \theta\neq0.
\end{cases}
}
$$
Together with (2),
$$
\boxed{
G(x)
=
G_t(\alpha(t)x+\beta(t)).
}
$$
This proves the result.

$\textbf{Note:}$
This exercise is a special case of Weissman's result.
In the original paper, Weissman does not assume that every limiting
distribution $G_t$ (or, in his notation, every $Z_t$) is non-degenerate.
In our exercise, however, non-degeneracy of $G_t$ is assumed for every
$t>0$.
Because of this stronger assumption, convergence to types immediately gives
$$
T=(0,\infty),
$$
whereas Weissman's original proof needs additional facts to establish which
$t$ belong to $T$.
If we try to solve this problem only by separately tracking the scale and
location terms, the error produced by
$$
[[nt]s]
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
[nts]
$$
is difficult to organize.
Weissman's useful idea is to package the scale and location normalizations
together into the positive affine group $H$:
$$
\gamma_n(t)
=
h_nh_{[nt]}^{-1}.
$$
Then the floor error is itself represented by a group element,
$$
h_{[[nt]s]}h_{[nts]}^{-1},
$$
and the statement
$$
h_nh_{n+g}^{-1}\to e
$$
for bounded integer shifts $g$ makes this error disappear asymptotically.
Thus the abstraction is not only notation. It packages two coupled
normalization errors into one object for which composition and inversion are
natural.
It is a fantastic experience that an exercise in the book may require us to
read the original paper in order to understand the method properly.
It also reminds us that we should not have the fantasy that all exercises in
an advanced book must be solvable using only the knowledge explicitly
developed in that book. Some exercises may come from deeper results or
original papers, and part of studying them is learning when additional
mathematical machinery is genuinely needed.

### Ex 29
::: problem

Suppose $\{X_t,t\geq0\}$ is a family of random variables parameterized by a
continuous variable $t$ and assume there exist normalizing constants
$a(t)>0$, $b(t)\in\mathbb R$ such that as $t\to\infty$

$$
\frac{X_t-b(t)}{a(t)}
\Rightarrow Y,
$$

where $Y$ is non-degenerate. Show the normalizing functions can always be
assumed continuous; that is, there exist continuous functions
$\alpha(t)>0$, $\beta(t)\in\mathbb R$ such that

$$
\frac{X_t-\beta(t)}{\alpha(t)}
\Rightarrow Y',
$$

where $Y'$ has a non-degenerate distribution.

(Hint: The convergence to types theorem provides normalizing constants which
can be smoothed by integration.)

:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

As stated, the exercise appears to be false.

Let

$$
Z\sim N(0,1),
$$

and define

$$
c(t)
=
\begin{cases}
1, & t\in\mathbb Q,\\
2, & t\notin\mathbb Q.
\end{cases}
$$

Set

$$
X_t=c(t)Z.
$$

Take

$$
a(t)=c(t),
\qquad
b(t)=0.
$$

Then, for every $t\geq0$,

$$
\frac{X_t-b(t)}{a(t)}
=
\frac{c(t)Z}{c(t)}
=
Z.
$$

Therefore

$$
\frac{X_t-b(t)}{a(t)}
\Rightarrow Z
$$

as $t\to\infty$, where $Z$ is non-degenerate. Thus all the assumptions of the
exercise are satisfied.

We now show that continuous normalizing functions cannot exist.

Suppose, to the contrary, that there exist continuous functions

$$
\alpha(t)>0,
\qquad
\beta(t)\in\mathbb R
$$

such that

$$
\frac{X_t-\beta(t)}{\alpha(t)}
\Rightarrow Y'
$$

for some non-degenerate random variable $Y'$.

Choose a sequence of rational numbers

$$
r_n\to\infty.
$$

Since $r_n\in\mathbb Q$,

$$
X_{r_n}=Z,
$$

and hence

$$
\frac{Z-\beta(r_n)}{\alpha(r_n)}
\Rightarrow Y'.
\tag{1}
$$

Since $Z$ is non-degenerate and $Y'$ is non-degenerate, the convergence to
types theorem applied to (1) implies that there exist constants

$$
A>0,
\qquad
B\in\mathbb R
$$

such that

$$
\alpha(r_n)\to A
$$

and

$$
\beta(r_n)\to B.
\tag{2}
$$

Moreover,

$$
Y'
\overset{d}{=}
\frac{Z-B}{A}.
\tag{3}
$$

Now use the continuity of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

For each $n$, since both functions are continuous at $r_n$, there exists
$\delta_n>0$ such that whenever

$$
|s-r_n|<\delta_n,
$$

we have

$$
|\alpha(s)-\alpha(r_n)|<\frac1n
$$

and

$$
|\beta(s)-\beta(r_n)|<\frac1n.
$$

Because the irrational numbers are dense in $\mathbb R$, we can choose an
irrational number $s_n$ satisfying

$$
|s_n-r_n|
<
\min\left(\delta_n,\frac1n\right).
$$

Then

$$
s_n\to\infty,
$$

and, by construction,

$$
\alpha(s_n)-\alpha(r_n)\to0,
$$

and

$$
\beta(s_n)-\beta(r_n)\to0.
$$

Together with (2),

$$
\alpha(s_n)\to A
$$

and

$$
\beta(s_n)\to B.
\tag{4}
$$

However, $s_n$ is irrational, so

$$
X_{s_n}=2Z.
$$

Therefore

$$
\frac{X_{s_n}-\beta(s_n)}{\alpha(s_n)}
=
\frac{2Z-\beta(s_n)}{\alpha(s_n)}
\Rightarrow
\frac{2Z-B}{A}.
$$

But by the assumed convergence along all $t\to\infty$, the same sequence must
converge to $Y'$. Hence

$$
Y'
\overset{d}{=}
\frac{2Z-B}{A}.
\tag{5}
$$

Combining (3) and (5),

$$
\frac{Z-B}{A}
\overset{d}{=}
\frac{2Z-B}{A}.
$$

This is impossible. Indeed,

$$
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
\frac{Z-B}{A}
\right)
=
\frac1{A^2},
$$

whereas

$$
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
\frac{2Z-B}{A}
\right)
=
\frac4{A^2}.
$$

Since $A>0$, the two distributions cannot be equal.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\text{Exercise 29 is false under the assumptions as printed.}
}
$$

$\textbf{Note:}$

The hint suggests smoothing the original normalizers by integration, for
example,

$$
\alpha(t)
=
\int_t^{t+1}a(s)\,ds,
\qquad
\beta(t)
=
\int_t^{t+1}b(s)\,ds.
$$

However, under the assumptions stated in the exercise, there is no reason
that these smoothed normalizers should be asymptotically equivalent to the
original normalizers.

The counterexample above shows that this is not merely a missing step in the
proof. Some additional regularity condition would be needed to make the
conclusion true.

Rather than adding such a condition ourselves, we leave the exercise in its
printed form and record the counterexample.


### Ex 3
::: problem

Suppose $\{U_n,n\geq1\}$ are iid $U(0,1)$ random variables so that

$$
P[U_j\leq x]=x,\qquad 0\leq x\leq1.
$$

(a) Show

$$
\prod_{j=1}^n U_j^{1/n}
$$

converges almost surely. What is the limit?

(b) Center and scale the sequence

$$
\left\{
\prod_{j=1}^n U_j^{1/n},\ n\geq1
\right\}
$$

and show the resulting sequence converges in distribution to a non-degenerate limit. To which one?

:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

#### (a)

Take logarithms:

$$
\log\left(
\prod_{j=1}^n U_j^{1/n}
\right)
=
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\log U_j.
$$

Since $\{U_j\}$ are iid, so are $\{\log U_j\}$.

Also,

$$
E|\log U_1|
=
\int_0^1 |\log x|\,dx
<
\infty.
$$

Therefore, by the SLLN,

$$
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\log U_j
\overset{a.s.}{\longrightarrow}
E(\log U_1).
$$

Now

$$
E(\log U_1)
=
\int_0^1\log x\,dx.
$$

Using integration by parts,

$$
\int \log x\,dx
=
x\log x-x,
$$

so

$$
E(\log U_1)
=
\left[x\log x-x\right]_0^1
=
-1.
$$

Hence

$$
\log\left(
\prod_{j=1}^n U_j^{1/n}
\right)
\overset{a.s.}{\longrightarrow}
-1.
$$

Since the exponential function is continuous,

$$
\boxed{
\prod_{j=1}^n U_j^{1/n}
\overset{a.s.}{\longrightarrow}
e^{-1}.
}
$$

#### (b)

Let

$$
L_n
=
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\log U_j.
$$

From part (a),

$$
E(\log U_1)=-1.
$$

We also have

$$
E\left[(\log U_1)^2\right]
=
\int_0^1(\log x)^2\,dx.
$$

Using integration by parts,

$$
\int (\log x)^2\,dx
=
x(\log x)^2
-
2x\log x
+
2x,
$$

and therefore

$$
E\left[(\log U_1)^2\right]
=
2.
$$

Thus

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\log U_1)
=
2-(-1)^2
=
1.
$$

By the CLT,

$$
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(L_n-(-1)\right)
}{
\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\log U_1)}
}
\Rightarrow
N(0,1).
$$

Since $\operatorname{Var}(\log U_1)=1$,

$$
\boxed{
\sqrt n(L_n+1)
\Rightarrow
N(0,1).
}
\tag{1}
$$

Now define

$$
g(x)=e^x.
$$

Then

$$
\prod_{j=1}^n U_j^{1/n}
=
e^{L_n}
=
g(L_n),
$$

and

$$
g(-1)=e^{-1},
\qquad
g'(-1)=e^{-1}.
$$

Applying the delta method to (1),

$$
\sqrt n
\left(
e^{L_n}-e^{-1}
\right)
\Rightarrow
e^{-1}N(0,1).
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{
\displaystyle
\prod_{j=1}^n U_j^{1/n}-e^{-1}
}{
e^{-1}/\sqrt n
}
\Rightarrow
N(0,1).
}
$$
